decisions.brief: brief-js163.md with js163-measurements.md, and the owner's direction of 2026-11-21 (detect the hardware and choose the best configuration automatically; fine-tuning allowed, never needed). On both UHD 630 nodes, in Jellyfin's image with jellyfin-ffmpeg, a 4K HDR re-encode done wholly on the GPU ran at 3.9 to 5.2 times real time for 0.16 to 0.28 CPU-seconds per second of film (4.1 to 7.2 on the processors), three at once at 1.5 to 2.0x each (video-processor tone map rows), at 0.97 to 1.47 times x264's bytes for equal SSIM on two fairly dark scenes; with an OpenCL tone map, one job at 3.85 to 3.97x for 0.5 to 0.7. No GPU tone map gives today's picture: the video processors' are about two thirds darker (VAAPI) and a third brighter (QSV) with no parameters; OpenCL with the hable curve is about a quarter darker, the same as jellyfin-ffmpeg's processor tone map. Today's colour tag options fail after GPU decode in ffmpeg 8; the same tags in the bitstream work.
decisions.tradeoff: Whether hardware encoding enters ahead of its place in the road, and what picture a viewer may be given for the speed: every measured GPU path changes an HDR film's brightness from the processor's.
decisions.entry: BL-040 is promoted on D-044's own reopen clause (a UHD 630 holds the job at 1.2x within twice x264's bytes), not on the request. JS-169 (measure, in jellyscale's own image, whether a GPU tone map with a set curve reaches the processor's picture; bytes on a bright scene and by a second measure; memory and jobs at once; the seam) enters at 20 and may run beside the builds ahead of it. JS-170 (first slice: Intel VAAPI/QSV, detected by a real test of each stage at start, chosen per job, processor otherwise) enters at 27 after JS-041 and JS-157, and moves to directly after JS-166 if JS-166 does not close the stall on processors or the dogfood counts a refusal for cores with every worker running. JS-054 keeps NVIDIA, AMD, hardware decode for processor streams and outputs above 1080 lines. 'Best configuration' is a rule of outcomes: the same picture first, then holding 1.2 times real time as measured on that worker, then no more than twice x264's bytes in a quality-targeted mode, then the least processor; otherwise the processor for that job, with the reason logged and counted (the HD 530 is the negative case). One film has one picture whatever the hardware: the driver video-processor tone maps are never used, by default or by override; a GPU tone map is accepted only within 5% (or one 8-bit code value, whichever is more) of the processor path's brightness above black and at SSIM 0.99 or above on three scenes; if no setting reaches that, the options return as a brief, among them moving the processor path to the shared curve, which would be a changed guarantee and is not taken here. Operators may set per worker hardware off, the device and the most hardware jobs at once, and nothing else; none is needed. Given up, by operators: the speed the video-processor tone maps have over the candidate path (up to a third) and their lower processor cost (0.16 to 0.28 CPU-seconds per second against 0.5 to 0.7, so 2 to 4 times), and with it some of the jobs one GPU node holds at once (three were measured on the rejected path, none yet on the candidate). Nothing by viewers. Unverified when decided: every figure in jellyscale's own image; the byte bound beyond two dark scenes of one film (SSIM margin about 0.0003); memory per job; the GPUs shared with other apps; whether any setting matches the picture; what brightness difference viewers notice (the 5% is the product owner's, to be argued with frames). Data that reopens it: JS-169 showing no path within the bound, or bytes past twice x264's on a bright scene; an operator's measured case where the automatic choice was wrong.

decisions.entry: JS-166 runs a processor worker on the 12-thread node beside the 4-core node's worker, which stays as helper and failover; no worker goes on the 6-processor node until it can use its GPU. decisions.entry: A helper is never claimed by a worker that is running a viewer's, a seek's or a failover's job of its spec, and with one worker no helper is queued or claimed whatever its free cores; a worker running only helpers of the spec may still take another after the one-second wait when it has the cores. JS-168 criterion 6 is made exact so, the older checks stand unamended but for one subcase (D-053), and docs/transcoding.md and DOMAINS.md invariant 58 state the rule. Rejected: allowing same-worker helpers (C: ten checks amended for a speed-up nobody measured); measuring first (D: holds a merge for an answer that would not change what lands); forbidding every second job of a spec on a worker (A: could take a large worker's second helper, unverified whether the 2+6 runs used one). Given up: the same-worker helper a lone worker with room for three jobs got before JS-168, read from the old code and never measured, by nobody known. Unverified when decided: whether a same-worker helper speeds a slow job on a worker with idle cores; whether any JS-168 long run had a helper beside a viewer's job on one worker (such a row is run again, holding nothing). Data that reopens it: a measurement of a same-worker helper reaching 1.0x on idle cores; the dogfood showing a job under 1.2x on a worker with the job's cost free and no other worker to help.

decisions.brief: brief-d052-capacity.md: one check unchanged since 30af59c (the 'not queued' half of the helper capacity check) wants a helper row queued on a lone 16-core worker holding 3.2 cores, which D-052's lone-worker rule forbids; on a trial of D-052 it fails with 0 rows, want 1; its 4-core case and its 'not claimed' sibling pass. Options: A (give the 16-core subcase a second worker running nothing of the spec and want the row there), B (keep the check, a lone worker helps itself), C (hold the fix for a measurement).
decisions.tradeoff: D-052 said every check that passed on 30af59c passes unamended; one subcase asserts exactly what D-052 gave up, so no build passes both.
decisions.serves: JS-168 criterion 6: 'with one worker nothing changes: no helper is queued or claimed, whatever cores the worker has free'. PRODUCT.md: 'A heavy film uses the whole cluster's processors rather than stalling on one machine while others sit idle.' docs/transcoding.md: 'No helper can start with one worker.'
decisions.entry: The 16-core subcase of the helper capacity check gains a second 16-core worker running nothing of the spec and wants the helper queued for it; the 4-core subcase and the 'not claimed' check are unchanged, and the amended case still fails on a build that queues nothing. It is the one exception to D-052's 'older checks stand unamended', named in JS-168 criterion 6 and cited as D-053 in Changed guarantees; any other old check that contradicts D-052 comes back as its own brief. The three JS-168 waits return to their 30af59c text (two helpers beside the main job) as a consequence of D-052, not an amendment. Rejected: B (reopens the regression D-052 closes; no rule separating a large lone worker from it is designed or measured); C (holds a merge for a measurement, rejected in D-052 and by the owner on 2026-11-21). Given up: the check's assertion that a lone worker with the cores queues a helper for itself, by operators of one large worker with transcodeHelpers on, number unknown, who were already told a lone worker gets no helper; the dogfood's 4-core case is unchanged. Unverified when decided: whether that queued row was ever claimed on a real film or sped one (the check shows a queued row only). Data that reopens it, as D-052: a measurement of a same-worker helper reaching 1.0x on idle cores; the dogfood showing a job under 1.2x on a worker with the job's cost free and no other worker to help.
